Definition: to commiserate; by implication, to spare
BiblicalUsage: Chamal is the word for sparing someone when you could destroy them, and it runs both ways in Scripture. Saul spared Agag and the best of the sheep when God had said destroy them all, and Pharaoh's daughter had compassion on the baby Moses in the bulrushes and spared his life. Nathan's parable turns on the same word: the rich man had no pity and would not spare his own flock, taking the poor man's lamb instead. Most often it is God who spares, or refuses to spare, and the word carries the weight of a decision, not a passing feeling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows me that mercy is a choice with consequences, not a soft mood. Saul's sparing looked kind and cost him the kingdom, while God's sparing in Malachi falls on those who fear Him and serve Him. I hold that true pity never overrules what God has said is right, and that is why I want my compassion shaped by His word rather than by my feelings in the moment.
